title: The leader next door, and the ones without stores
lede: Nearly every Hollywood Video had a Blockbuster close by. The competitors that mattered in the end had no stores at all.

blocks.title: Who won, who died
blocks.subtitle: The rental chains of 2004 and the service that replaced them.

items.name: Hollywood Video
items.text: Sold to Movie Gallery in 2005 and liquidated in 2010. The name survives on a blog.[^5][^19][^22]

items.name: Blockbuster
items.text: The leader, with 9,094 stores worldwide. Bid for Hollywood and withdrew. Filed for Chapter 11 on September 23, 2010.[^9][^23][^24]

items.name: Movie Gallery
items.text: The buyer. 4,749 stores after the merger, Chapter 11 in 2007 and 2010, then liquidation.[^11][^13][^19]

items.name: Netflix
items.text: Rental by mail, with no stores. Subscribers went from 857,000 at the end of 2002 to 6.3 million at the end of 2006.[^25]

blocks.source: Store counts from the companies’ annual reports[^5][^11][^13][^23]; Movie Gallery’s February 2010 figure is from Bloomberg News[^15]. Netflix subscribers in thousands.[^25] The series are not on a common scale.

blocks.title: Stores at the end of 2004
blocks.subtitle: The three chains in the takeover fight, just before it was settled.
blocks.source: Blockbuster[^23], Movie Gallery[^11] and Hollywood Entertainment[^5] annual reports. The bases differ slightly, as noted on each bar.
Hollywood Entertainment[^5], Blockbuster[^23][^24] and Movie Gallery[^13] filings; the Associated Press.[^9]

blocks.text: Substantially all of our stores compete with stores operated by Blockbuster, most in very close proximity.

blocks.body: The Associated Press reported in 2005 that regulators had blocked a Blockbuster–Hollywood combination once before, in 1999.[^9] We did not find a primary record of that earlier episode and give it only on the AP’s authority.
